ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.error: Puts the plural -s on the last part of a hyphenated compound (mother-in-laws, passer-bys).

example.question: My two ___ came to the party.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.reveals: Offer "mother-in-laws" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.help: The main noun takes the plural: mothers, then in-law.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.feedback: In a hyphenated compound the main noun takes the plural: mothers-in-law, passers-by, not mother-in-laws.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.error: Writes a one-word compound as two words (tooth brush, class room) or the other way round.

example.question: Wanjiru bought a new ___.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.reveals: Offer "tooth brush" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.help: Check the dictionary: some compounds are one word, some two.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.feedback: Some compound nouns are one word (toothbrush, classroom), some are two (post office), and some have a hyphen (mother-in-law). Look in a dictionary.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.error: Leaves a compound noun singular where a plural is needed.

example.question: The ___ sell stamps.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.reveals: Offer "post office" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.help: Ask: one or many? Many needs the plural -s on the main noun.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.feedback: Many post offices sell stamps. Put the plural on the main noun.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T1_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.error: Uses the wrong collective noun for a group (a herd of fish, a swarm of lions).

example.question: A ___ of lions rested under the tree.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.cause: Uses one word for every group.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.reveals: Offer "swarm" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.help: Each group has its own word.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.feedback: Each kind of group has its own collective noun: a pride of lions, a school of fish, a fleet of ships, a troop of monkeys, a crew of sailors.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.error: Writes the collective noun as a plural (a flocks of birds, a crews of sailors).

example.question: A ___ of sailors boarded the ship.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.reveals: Offer "crews" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.help: One group is one thing, so one crew.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.feedback: A collective noun names one group, so write a crew of sailors, not a crews of sailors.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.error: Leaves out of after the collective noun (a swarm bees).

example.question: A swarm ___ bees settled on the roof.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.reveals: Offer "for" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.help: The words go: a swarm of bees.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.feedback: Say a swarm of bees. The collective noun is followed by of.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T2_WORD_CLASSES_COLLECT.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.error: Puts an apostrophe in a plain plural (apple's for sale, the boy's are here).

example.question: Mama bought three ___ at the market.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.reveals: Offer "mango's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.help: A plain plural does not take an apostrophe.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.feedback: An apostrophe shows belonging or a short form, not a plural: three mangoes, not three mango's.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.error: Puts the apostrophe in the wrong place for belonging (the boys book, the boy's books for many boys).

example.question: The ___ bags are in the classroom. (many boys)

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.reveals: Offer "boy's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.help: One owner: 's. Many owners ending in s: s'.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.feedback: For one owner write the boy's bag. For many owners write the boys' bags, with the apostrophe after the s.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.error: Leaves out the commas in a list or puts one before the last item wrongly.

example.question: We bought rice___ beans and maize.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.reveals: Offer "" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.help: Separate the items in a list with commas.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.feedback: Put a comma between the items of a list and use and before the last: rice, beans and maize.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: The cow licked ___ calf.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.reveals: Offer "it's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.help: It's means it is. Its shows belonging.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.feedback: Its (no apostrophe) shows belonging: its calf. It's is short for it is or it has.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T2_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.error: Does not make has, have or do agree with the subject (she have finished, they has gone).

example.question: Wanjiru ___ finished her work.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.reveals: Offer "have" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.help: He, she and it take has; I, you, we and they take have.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.feedback: Use has with he, she, it and one name (Wanjiru has). Use have with I, you, we and they.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.error: Uses the wrong form of be (they was playing, I is ready).

example.question: The boys ___ playing football.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.reveals: Offer "was" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.help: Many people or things take were or are.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.feedback: Use was with I, he, she and it, and were with you, we, they and plural nouns: The boys were playing.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.error: Puts did or does and then a past or -s verb (did went, does goes).

example.question: Otieno did not ___ to school.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.reveals: Offer "went" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.help: After did and does the main verb stays plain.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.feedback: After do, does or did the main verb has no ending: Otieno did not go, he does not go.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T3_WORD_CLASSES_PRIMARY.A.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.error: Mixes a stanza and a line of a poem.

example.question: What is a stanza?
example.correct_answer: A group of lines in a poem

ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.reveals: Offer "One line of a poem" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.help: A stanza is like a paragraph of lines.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.feedback: A line is one row of words in a poem. A stanza is a group of lines.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: What is repetition in a poem?
example.wrong_answer: Words with the same end sound
example.correct_answer: A word or line said again

ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.reveals: Offer "Words with the same end sound" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.help: Rhyme is the same sound. Repetition is the same words again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.feedback: Rhyme is words with the same end sound. Repetition is a word or a line said again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.error: Says the speaker of a poem is always the poet.

example.question: Who is the persona in a poem?
example.correct_answer: The voice that speaks in the poem

ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.reveals: Offer "The poet himself, always" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.help: The speaker may be an imagined person.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.feedback: The persona is the voice that speaks in the poem. It may be the poet or an imagined person.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T3_INTENSIVE_READING_PO.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.error: Leaves out the -s after he, she or it in the simple present (he walk, she like).

example.question: Achieng ___ to school every day.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.reveals: Offer "walk" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.help: One name or he, she or it adds -s in the present.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.feedback: In the simple present add -s or -es after he, she, it or one name: Achieng walks.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.error: Puts the past form after did or did not (did not went, did she saw).

example.question: Baraka did not ___ the answer.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.reveals: Offer "knew" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.help: After did the verb is plain.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.feedback: Did already shows the past, so the verb stays plain: did not know, did she see.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.error: Adds -ed to an irregular verb or uses the wrong irregular form (goed, eated, seen for saw).

example.question: Yesterday we ___ to the market.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.reveals: Offer "goed" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.help: Irregular verbs have their own past form.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.feedback: Irregular verbs do not add -ed. Learn the forms: go, went; see, saw; eat, ate; run, ran.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T4_VERBS_AND_TENSE.PRESEN.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.error: Uses very or more with a non-gradable adjective (very perfect, more unique, very dead).

example.question: The soup is ___ perfect.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.reveals: Offer "very" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.help: Perfect, empty and dead cannot be more or less.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.feedback: A non-gradable adjective such as perfect, empty, dead or unique cannot be graded, so use absolutely or completely, not very.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.error: Uses absolutely or completely with a gradable adjective (absolutely tall, completely cold).

example.question: The boy is ___ tall for his age.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.reveals: Offer "absolutely" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.help: Tall can be more or less. Very goes with it.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.feedback: A gradable adjective such as tall, cold or big can be more or less, so use very, quite or extremely with it.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.error: Makes a degree form of a non-gradable adjective (most unique, more empty, deader).

example.question: This painting is ___.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.reveals: Offer "more unique" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.help: Unique means one of a kind, so it has no degrees.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.feedback: Unique, perfect, empty and dead have no comparative or superlative form. Say unique, not more unique.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T5_WORD_CLASSES_ADJECTI.G.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.error: Puts the frequency adverb in the wrong place (She arrives always, he never is late).

example.question: Achieng ___ to school early.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.reveals: Offer "comes always" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.help: Put the adverb before the main verb and after be.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.feedback: A frequency adverb goes before the main verb (she always comes) and after be (he is never late).
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.error: Uses too where very is meant (too good, too beautiful).

example.question: The mandazi were ___ tasty, so we ate them all.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.reveals: Offer "too" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.help: Too means more than is wanted. Very just adds strength.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.feedback: Too means more than enough and is usually a problem (too hot to drink). Use very for a strong degree: very tasty.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.error: Uses never with not (does not never come, I do not never go).

example.question: She ___ comes late.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.reveals: Offer "does not never" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.feedback: Never already makes the sentence negative, so do not add not: she never comes late.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T6_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS.F.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.error: Misspells a commonly misspelt word (seperate, definately, neccessary).

example.question: Please ___ the red beans from the green ones.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.reveals: Offer "seperate" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.help: Look for the a in the middle: sep-a-rate.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.feedback: Learn the tricky spellings: separate, definitely, necessary, occasion, accommodate, tomorrow. Look at the word, cover it, write it, check it.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.error: Writes ei where ie is needed or the other way round (beleive, recieve).

example.question: We ___ a letter from Nairobi.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.reveals: Offer "recieve" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.help: I before e, except after c.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.feedback: Write i before e except after c: believe, but receive and ceiling. A few words break the rule, such as seize and weird.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.error: Doubles a letter that should not be doubled or leaves out a double letter (acommodate, occassion).

example.question: The hotel can ___ forty guests.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.reveals: Offer "acommodate" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.help: Accommodate has two c and two m.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.feedback: Accommodate has a double c and a double m. Occasion has a double c and one s.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T6_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING.S.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.error: Writes hisself or theirselves for himself and themselves.

example.question: The boys taught ___ to swim.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.reveals: Offer "theirselves" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.help: The reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.feedback: The reflexive forms are myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves and themselves. There is no theirselves or hisself.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.error: Writes ourself or yourselfs where the plural -selves is needed.

example.question: We made the cake ___.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.reveals: Offer "ourself" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.feedback: Plural reflexive pronouns end in -selves: ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.error: Treats everyone, someone or nobody as plural (everyone are here, nobody are hurt).

example.question: Everyone ___ ready for the trip.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.reveals: Offer "are" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.help: Everyone is one word, so it is singular.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.feedback: Everyone, someone, anybody and nobody take a singular verb: everyone is ready.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T7_WORD_CLASSES_PRONOUN.I.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.error: Uses the wrong preposition of time (at Monday, in 6 o'clock, on June).

example.question: The sports day is ___ Friday.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.cause: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.reveals: Offer "in" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.help: On for days, in for months and years, at for clock times.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.feedback: Use on with days (on Friday), in with months, years and parts of the day (in June, in the morning) and at with clock times (at 6 o'clock).
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.error: Uses beside for between, or between for many things (between the boys in the class).

example.question: The ball is ___ the two goal posts.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.reveals: Offer "beside" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.feedback: Between is for two (or a few named) things and beside means next to: the ball is between the two posts.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.error: Uses in for a point or a surface (in the gate, in the table).

example.question: Otieno waited ___ the school gate.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.reveals: Offer "in" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.help: At is for a point, on for a surface, in for inside.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.feedback: Use at for a point (at the gate), on for a surface (on the table) and in for inside a space (in the room).
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T8_WORD_CLASSES_SIMPLE_.P.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.error: Uses although and but together (Although it rained, but we played).

example.question: ___ it was raining, we played football.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.reveals: Offer "Although but" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.feedback: Although and but both show a contrast, so use only one of them: Although it was raining, we played.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.error: Uses because and so together (Because he was late, so he ran).

example.question: Because Juma was late, ___ he ran to school.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.reveals: Offer "so" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.feedback: Because and so both join a reason and a result. Use one: Because Juma was late, he ran. Or: Juma was late, so he ran.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.error: Uses unless with a negative (unless you do not study).

example.question: You will fail ___ you study.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.reveals: Offer "unless you do not" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.feedback: Unless means if not, so do not add not: You will fail unless you study.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.error: Picks a conjunction whose meaning does not fit (because for a contrast, unless for a reason).

example.question: ___ it was raining, we played football.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.reveals: Offer "Because" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.help: Ask what the two parts of the sentence say to each other: a reason, a contrast, a condition.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.feedback: Choose the conjunction for the meaning: because for a reason, although for a contrast, unless for a condition, until for a limit in time, while for two things at once, so for a result.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T9_WORD_CLASSES_CONJUNC.C.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.error: Calls a comparison with like or as a metaphor.

example.question: He ran like the wind. What figure of speech is this?

ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.reveals: Offer "metaphor" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.feedback: A simile compares two things using like or as: he ran like the wind.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.error: Calls a direct comparison a simile (The boy is a lion).

example.question: The boy is a lion in the game. What figure of speech is this?

ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.reveals: Offer "simile" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.help: A metaphor says one thing is another, without like or as.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.feedback: A metaphor says one thing is another without like or as: the boy is a lion.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.error: Takes the comparison word for word (He is a lion means he is an animal).

example.question: He is a lion in the game. What does it mean?

ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.reveals: Offer "He is a real animal" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.help: Ask what quality the two share.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.feedback: A metaphor uses a picture to show a quality: a lion is brave, so he is brave and strong.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T9_INTENSIVE_READING_SI.S.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..error: Uses this with a plural noun or these with a singular noun (this books, these book).

example.question: ___ books on my desk are mine.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..reveals: Offer "This" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..help: This is one; these is many.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..feedback: Use this and that with one thing, and these and those with many things: these books.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..error: Uses this or these for something far away, or that or those for something near.

example.question: The teacher points at a tree across the field: ___ tree is tall.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..reveals: Offer "This" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..help: This and these are near; that and those are far.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..feedback: This and these point to things near the speaker. That and those point to things far away.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..error: Uses much with a count noun or many with a non-count noun.

example.question: There are too ___ cars on the road.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..reveals: Offer "much" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..help: Cars can be counted, so many.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..feedback: Use many and few with nouns we count (many cars) and much and little with nouns we cannot count (much traffic).
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T10_WORD_CLASSES_DEMONST..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..error: Uses an adjective where the adverb is needed (she sings good, he ran quick, the baby smiled happy).

example.question: Wanjiru sings very ___.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..reveals: Offer "good" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..help: Good describes a noun. Well describes a verb.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..feedback: The adverb of good is well: she sings well. Good is an adjective: a good song.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..error: Spells the -ly adverb wrongly (happyly, gentlely, truely).

example.question: The baby smiled ___.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..reveals: Offer "happyly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..help: After a consonant, change y to i before -ly; -le becomes -ly; true becomes truly.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..feedback: Change y to i before -ly (happily), change -le to -ly (gently) and write truly, not truely.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..error: Uses hardly for hard or lately for late.

example.question: Otieno studied ___ for the test.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..reveals: Offer "hardly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..help: Hardly means almost not. The adverb of hard is hard.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..feedback: Hard, fast and late are also adverbs without -ly. Hardly means almost not at all and lately means recently.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T11_WORD_CLASSES_ADVERBS..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..error: Uses the wrong prefix (unagree, disinteresting where uninteresting is meant).

example.question: The boys had a ___ about the rules.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..reveals: Offer "unagreement" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..help: Dis- goes with agree, un- goes with happy.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..feedback: Words take their own prefix: disagree, unhappy, replay, misunderstand. Check in a dictionary.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..error: Gives the wrong meaning to a prefix or suffix (careless means full of care).

example.question: What does careless mean?

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..reveals: Offer "full of care" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..feedback: The suffix -ful means full of and -less means without: careful is full of care, careless is without care.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..error: Spells the new word wrongly when adding a suffix (happyness, beautifull).

example.question: Kindness and ___ are good values.

ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..reveals: Offer "happyness" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..help: Change y to i before the ending -ness.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..feedback: When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i before the suffix: happiness. The suffix -ful has one l: beautiful.
ENGL.G8.WRITIN.T11_MECHANICS_OF_WRITING..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.error: Gives the wrong meaning of a phrasal verb (give up means present, run out of means run away).

example.question: The man gave up smoking. What did he do?

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.reveals: Offer "He gave it to someone" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.help: Read the whole sentence for the meaning.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.feedback: A phrasal verb has its own meaning: give up means stop, look after means take care of, run out of means have no more.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.error: Uses the wrong particle (look at the baby for look after, turn of the light).

example.question: Please ___ the light when you leave.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.reveals: Offer "turn on" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.help: The particle changes the meaning: on and off are opposites.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.feedback: The particle changes the meaning: turn on starts a light, turn off stops it.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.error: Reads a phrasal verb word by word (break down means break something).

example.question: The bus broke down near Nakuru. What happened?

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.reveals: Offer "It was broken into pieces" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.help: Think what the whole phrase means.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.feedback: A phrasal verb often has a meaning that is not the sum of its parts: break down means stop working.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T12_PHRASAL_VERBS.PHRASAL.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..error: Joins two sentences with only a comma (I was tired, I went to bed).

example.question: I was tired ___ I went to bed.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..reveals: Offer "," next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..help: A comma alone cannot join two sentences.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..feedback: Two complete sentences need a conjunction as well as the comma: I was tired, so I went to bed.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..error: Leaves out the comma before the conjunction (She ran fast but she lost).

example.question: She ran fast___ but she lost.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..reveals: Offer "" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..help: Put a comma before the joining word.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..feedback: A comma goes before for, and, nor, but, or, yet or so when it joins two sentences: She ran fast, but she lost.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..error: Chooses a conjunction that does not fit (It rained, and we stayed home when we wanted to go).

example.question: It was raining, ___ we stayed indoors.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..reveals: Offer "but" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..help: Think: does the second part show a result, a contrast or an addition?
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..feedback: Pick the conjunction for the meaning: so for a result, but and yet for a contrast, and for an addition, or for a choice.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T13_WORD_CLASSES_COMPOUN..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..error: Calls a plain description personification, or misses personification.

example.question: Which sentence has personification?
example.correct_answer: The wind whispered in my ear.

ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..reveals: Offer "The wind was strong." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..help: Does a thing act like a person?
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..feedback: Personification gives a thing or an animal a human action or feeling: the wind whispered.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..error: Says a flashback jumps forward in time.

example.question: What is a flashback?
example.wrong_answer: A jump to the future of the story
example.correct_answer: A return to an earlier time in the story

ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..reveals: Offer "A jump to the future of the story" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..feedback: A flashback takes the reader back to something that happened earlier.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: Which sentence has personification?
example.wrong_answer: The cloud was like a pillow.
example.correct_answer: The cloud smiled at the hills.

ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..reveals: Offer "The cloud was like a pillow." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..help: A simile compares with like or as. Personification gives human actions.
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..feedback: Personification gives a human action to a thing (the cloud smiled). A simile uses like or as (the cloud was like a pillow).
ENGL.G8.READIN.T13_SHORT_STORY_STYLE_CL..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..error: Picks a sounded letter as the silent one (in knife, says f).

example.question: Which letter is silent in knife?

ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..reveals: Offer "f" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..feedback: In knife the k is silent: we say /naɪf/.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..error: Picks the wrong silent letter in a word (castle: c, honest: n).

example.question: Which letter is silent in castle?

ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..reveals: Offer "c" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..feedback: In castle the t is silent. In honest the h is silent. In listen the t is silent.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..error: Leaves out the silent letter when spelling (nife, rite, ilsand).

example.question: Spell the word for a tool to cut with: ___.

ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..reveals: Offer "nife" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..help: Silent letters still appear when you write.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..feedback: A silent letter is not said but it is written: knife, write, island, castle, honest, lamb.
ENGL.G8.LISTEN.T14_PRONUNCIATION_AND_IN..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..error: Uses the wrong verb form in the passive (was bite, was wrote).

example.question: The boy was ___ by the dog.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..reveals: Offer "bite" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..help: The passive uses be and the past participle.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..feedback: The passive is formed with be and the past participle: was bitten, was written, was taken.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..error: Calls an active sentence passive, or the other way round.

example.question: Which sentence is passive: Juma kicked the ball. The ball was kicked by Juma.
example.correct_answer: The ball was kicked by Juma.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..reveals: Offer "Juma kicked the ball." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..help: In the passive the subject receives the action.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..feedback: In the active voice the subject does the action (Juma kicked the ball). In the passive the subject receives it (The ball was kicked by Juma).
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..error: Leaves out be in the passive (The boy bitten by the dog).

example.question: The window ___ broken by the wind.

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..reveals: Offer "(nothing)" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..help: The passive needs a form of be.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..feedback: A passive sentence needs a form of be before the past participle: The window was broken by the wind.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T14_SENTENCES_ACTIVE_AND..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..error: Gives a positive tag after a positive sentence (You are coming, are you).

example.question: You are coming, ___?

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..reveals: Offer "are you" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..help: A positive sentence takes a negative tag.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..feedback: A positive sentence takes a negative tag (You are coming, aren't you) and a negative sentence takes a positive tag (You are not coming, are you).
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..error: Uses isn't it for every tag (They are late, isn't it).

example.question: They are late, ___?

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..cause: Copied from the usual spoken Kenyan English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..reveals: Offer "isn't it" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..help: The tag repeats the helping verb and the subject.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..feedback: The tag repeats the helping verb and the subject as a pronoun: They are late, aren't they. Isn't it is not for every tag.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..error: Uses the wrong helping verb in the tag (She likes tea, isn't she).

example.question: She likes tea, ___?

ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..reveals: Offer "isn't she" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..help: Use the helping verb of the sentence: likes needs does.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..feedback: The tag uses the helping verb that fits the sentence: She likes tea, doesn't she. For present simple, use do or does.
ENGL.G8.GRAMMA.T15_TYPES_OF_SENTENCES_I..source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher
